To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that
serum levels of copper and cholesterol increase, and levels of zinc and carotenoids decrease, in the chick during the early stages of experimentally induced Newcastle disease.
serum copper, zinc and cholesterol concentrations were significantly increased and serum carotenoids and zinc concentrations significantly decreased in chickens experimentally infected with NDV.
the concentrations of serum copper, zinc and cholesterol were increased and that those of serum total carotenoids and serum zinc were reduced in experimentally induced Newcastle disease in chickens.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the possible use of these moieties as indicators of the early stages of the disease.
the effect of the virus infection on the metabolism of the chick.
a possible link between nutrition, immunity, and disease.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the changes in the concentrations of copper, zinc, carotenoids, and cholesterol in serum were not the cause but the consequence of the disease process.
the changes in serum copper, zinc and cholesterol values are a consequence of the disease process and not a cause of the disease.
serum copper, zinc and cholesterol values in the chick are affected by experimental Newcastle disease virus infection.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that

the serum copper concentration is a more sensitive indicator of the early effects of Newcastle disease virus than is either serum zinc or carotenoids, and the serum cholesterol concentration is more sensitive than any of the other moieties.

the serum concentrations of copper, zinc, total cholesterol, and total carotenoid were affected in a manner consistent with the development of disease, and that changes in these values were detectable before any overt signs were evident.
the serum values of copper, zinc, total carotenoid, and cholesterol are useful indicators of disease in the chick.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the concentrations of these moieties in serum can be altered by the presence of disease and that the changes may be detectable prior to the onset of overt clinical signs.
